```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(survey)
```
:::



A school wants to estimate the average score on a reading comprehension exam for sixth grade students. The school’s students are grouped into 3 tracks, based on their performance in reading classes in 5th grade. The school decides to stratify on tracks because this method should reduce the variability of test scores. The sixth grade contains a total of 55 students in track I, 80 in track II, and 65 in track III. A stratified random sample is taken with 14 students in track I, 20 students in track II, and 16 students in track III. 

The data for the **sample** of students are located in the file `10-sixthgrade.csv` file on canvas.

2.	Based on the plot you created, comment on the patterns you see with respect to center and variability. Do you think there could be a problem in placing students in tracks (for their learning)? Do you think that stratified sampling will be beneficial over SRS in this case?

:::{.version-solution}
*The reading comprehension scores definitely differ between the three strata! The variation within strata looks smaller than the overall variability between scores across all students. This means that we are going to see precision benefits for stratification over SRS in this case. However, I will note that educationally it is a bad idea to split up students based on performance!*

:::


## Estimation with Stratified Sampling

3. Fill in the table below:

:::callout-warning

Remember that the data that you have is the SAMPLE data! So this is just asking you to calculate the means and sds from the data, not take an additional sample.
:::


::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use R to calculate sample stratum means and sds
# hint: use group_by() and summarize()

readingdat |> 
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error in parse(text = input): <text>:6:0: unexpected end of input
4: readingdat |> 
5: 
  ^
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
strat_dat <- readingdat |> 
  group_by(track) |> 
  summarise(ybar_g = mean(scores),
            sd_g = sd(scores),
            N_g = first(size),
            n_g = n()) 

strat_dat |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|track | ybar_g|   sd_g| N_g| n_g|
|:-----|------:|------:|---:|---:|
|I     | 79.714| 10.254|  55|  14|
|II    | 64.750| 12.578|  80|  20|
|III   | 37.438| 13.643|  65|  16|


:::
:::


:::{.version-student .version-instructions}

$N =$

|TRACK | I |	II|	III|
|-----|---|---|----|
|$N_{g}$ | . |.  |.   |
|$n_{g}$	|. |. |. |		
|${\bar{y}}_{g}$		|. |. |. |		
|$s_{g}$		|. |. |. |		
:::

$N = 200$

4.	Use the appropriate equations to *estimate* the average score for the sixth grade (i.e. calculate $\bar{y}_{st}$). Do all the calculations by hand, only rounding it at the end to 3 significant decimal places. Show your work!


::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use R as a calculator if you want!
```
:::



::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(strat_dat$N_g*strat_dat$ybar_g)/sum(strat_dat$N_g)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 59.98862
```


:::
:::



:::{.version-solution}

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{y}_{st} &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{g=1}^L N_g\bar{y}_g\\
&= \frac{1}{200}\big[(55\times 79.714) +(80\times	64.750)+(65\times37.438) \big] \\
& \approx  59.989
\end{align}
$$

:::

5.	Now use the `survey` package in to calculate the standard error. Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the parameter of interest "by hand" using the mean and standard error and a critical value of 2. 



::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use the survey package!
# Hint: the SIZE variable in the data gives the N_gs
```
:::



::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
strat_des <- svydesign(ids = ~1,
                       strata = ~track,
                       fpc = ~ size,
                       data = readingdat)

svymean(~scores, design = strat_des, na.rm = T)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
         mean     SE
scores 59.989 1.5162
```


:::
:::


:::callout-warning
## Incorrect analysis

6.	Now use R to calculate the standard error and the 95% confidence interval for the parameter of interest, forgetting that you used a stratified design and **treating the study like an SRS**


::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# add a variable N that gives the overall population size to your data for use in the function

readingdat$N <- 200

# use the survey package!
```
:::



::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
readingdat$N <- 200
srs_des <- svydesign(ids = ~1,
                       fpc = ~ N,
                       data = readingdat)

svymean(~scores, design = srs_des, na.rm = T)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       mean     SE
scores 60.2 2.5475
```


:::
:::



:::

7. Was stratification beneficial to accuracy? Was that what you expected? Explain.

:::{.version-solution}

*Yes!! The precision was improved by the stratification (smaller standard error)*

:::


8. Estimate the average score for the *track I* students and the variance of that estimate.


::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use R for a calculator
```
:::


:::{.version-solution}

The estimate for the average score for track I students $\mu_1$, is just $\bar{y}_1 = 79.714$.

$$
\begin{align}
\hat{\mathbb{V}}[\bar{y}_1] &= \big(1-\frac{n_1}{N_1}\big)\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} \\
&= \big(1-\frac{14}{55}\big)\frac{10.25^2}{14} \\
&\approx 5.594
\end{align}
$$


If we wanted the CI as well:

$$\bar{y}_1 \pm 2 \times \sqrt{(1-\frac{n_1}{N_1})\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}}$$
$$79.714 \pm 2 \times \sqrt{(1-\frac{14}{55})\frac{10.25^2}{14}}$$
:::


::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use R for a calculator

(vhat <- (1-(14/55))*10.25^2/14)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 5.594237
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
se <- sqrt(vhat)

79.714 + 2*se
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 84.44443
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
79.714 - 2*se
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 74.98357
```


:::
:::


9.	Estimate the average score for the *track II* students and the variance of that estimate.


::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use R for a calculator
```
:::


:::{.version-solution}
The estimate for the average score for track II students $\mu_2$, is just $\bar{y}_2 = 64.75$.

$$
\begin{align}
\hat{\mathbb{V}}[\bar{y}_2] &= \big(1-\frac{n_2}{N_2}\big)\frac{s_2^2}{n_2} \\
&= \big(1-\frac{20}{80}\big)\frac{12.578^2}{20} \\
&\approx 5.93
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}

```

```

```

## Estimating Proportions

Say instead of an average score, the school was actually interested in estimating the **proportion** of students who will get a "passing" score of 60 or above.

10. What is our variable of interest now (i.e. $y_{gi}$)?

:::{.version-solution}
*The variable of interest is* **whether or not that student** *got a passing score of 60 points or above*

$$
y_{gi} =
  \begin{cases}
    1       & \quad \text{if student } i \text{ in track }g \text{ scored 60 or more} \\
    0      & \quad \text{if student } i \text{ in track }g \text{ scored less than 60}
  \end{cases}
$$

:::

11. Use the appropriate equations to *estimate* the *proportion* of for the sixth grade that will pass the reading comprehension test. Do all the calculations by hand, only rounding it at the end to 3 significant decimal places. Show your work!


::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use R to get strata sample proportions to use in the calculation
# hint: make a new variable called "passed" that is 1 if the student has a SCORES >= 60 and 0 if not
# hint: use group_by() and summarize()
```
:::



::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use R as a calculator if you want!
```
:::




::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
readingdat |> 
  mutate(passed = scores >= 60) |> 
  group_by(track) |> 
  summarize(phat_g = mean(passed))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  track phat_g
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 I      1    
2 II     0.6  
3 III    0.125
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
p_g <- c(1, 0.6, 0.125)
N_g <- strat_dat$N_g

sum(N_g*p_g)/sum(N_g)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.555625
```


:::
:::



:::{.version-solution}
$$
\begin{align}
\hat{p}_{st} &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{g=1}^L N_g\hat{p}_g\\
&= \frac{1}{200}\big[(55\times 1.0) +(80\times	0.60)+(65\times 0.125) \big] \\
& \approx  0.556
\end{align}
$$
:::

## Sample Size


12. Suppose the *average test score* for the class is to be estimated *again at the end of the school year* with a bound of four points on the error of estimation. The costs of sampling are equal in all strata, but the variances differ. Assume the variances are in line with what we saw in the study at the beginning of the year. Find the overall sample size and the sample size for each stratum using the *appropriate allocation*. Do all the calculations by hand and show your work.

Make sure that you make clear what your:

- allocation method
- allocations ($a_g$'s)
- overall sample size $n$
- and stratum sample sizes ($n_g$'s) are.


::: {.cell version='student'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# use R as a calculator if you want
```
:::



::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# population size
N <- 200
# for mean
D <- 4^2/4
# sigmas
sigma_g <- c(10.25, 12.58, 13.64)
# strata pop sizes
N_g <- c(55, 80, 65)

neym_numerator <- sum(N_g*sigma_g)^2
neym_denom <- (sum(N_g*(sigma_g^2))) + (N^2*D)

neym_numerator/neym_denom
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 31.6777
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ag <- N_g*sigma_g/sum(N_g*sigma_g)
ag
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.2294698 0.4096469 0.3608833
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell version='solution'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ag*32
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  7.343034 13.108701 11.548265
```


:::
:::


:::{.version-solution}

*We use Neyman allocation since the variances differ. We estimate an overall sample size of $n = 32$ students. We estimate the allocations between the tracks should be $a_1 = 0.23, a_2 = 0.41, a_3 = 0.36$. Therefore, we should sample $n_1 = 7$ students from Track I, $n_2 = 13$ students from Track II, and $n_3 = 12$ students from Track III.*

:::
